input: Feedback control is a cornerstone of modern process operations, and the humble flow loop provides a particularly clear and instructive illustration of how it works in practice. The purpose of a flow loop is to hold the flow in a line serving a process vessel at its desired set point by acting directly on the flow itself. At the heart of the loop sits the sensor, which measures the flow in the line and transmits the measured value to the controller on a continuous basis. It is worth noting that the loop acts on the reading rather than on the true flow, so any error in the sensor quietly propagates into every subsequent action. The controller then compares the measured value against the set point and calculates an appropriate correction based on the difference between them, which is known as the error. This output is passed to the final element, typically a control valve installed in the line, which adjusts its position in order to change the flow in the required direction. Crucially, the sign of the feedback is negative: a rise in flow above the set point drives the valve toward closed, while a fall below the set point drives it toward open, meaning that the correction always opposes the deviation that produced it. It is this negative character that confers stability on the loop as a structure, since each departure from the set point generates an action that works to reduce that very departure. The description here concerns structure rather than settings; how far the valve travels for a given error, and how quickly the loop responds, are matters of tuning, and no tuning values are given.
target: A flow loop holds the flow in a line serving a process vessel at its set point by acting on the flow itself. The sensor measures the flow in the line and sends the measured value to the controller. A flow sensor reads the rate continuously, and the reading, not the true flow, is what the loop acts on; a sensor error enters every action the loop takes. The controller compares the measured value with the set point and calculates the correction from the difference between them, the error. The controller output goes to the final element, a control valve in the line, which moves to change the flow in the direction the controller demands. The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in flow above the set point drives the valve toward closed, and a fall in flow below the set point drives the valve toward open, so the correction opposes the deviation that produced it. Negative feedback is what makes the loop stable in structure: each departure from the set point generates an action that reduces the departure. The loop as described is structure only. How far the valve moves for a given error, and how fast the loop responds, are settings, and no settings are stated here. The vessel the line serves receives the result of the loop as a steady inflow; disturbances entering with the flow are corrected in the line itself, before they reach the vessel as a changed charge rate.
